projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Felix Magier was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Five nineteen, Ed LoBuglio's house, interviewing Felix Magier, who was born on January 27, 1924. Currently lives at 15463 Mount Eaton Road, Rittman, Ohio. Ed is the grandson of Felix Magier, who is a first class torpedoman in the Navy during World War II and the Korean War and his boat was stationed in the Pacific Ocean. Were you -- did you enlist or were you drafted?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: I was drafted.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Were you willing to be drafted?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Where were you living at the time?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: I was living in Barton, Ohio.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: What was the first day that you were called into the service?

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Was that the first day you were in training camp or the first day you were on the ship?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: The first -- no, no, no. I went to boot camp for three months. That's where you go to learn about the Navy and so on and so forth.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: What did you feel about it?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Did you like it or not?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. It was all right. It got a little rough at times and exercising every morning and so on and so forth if you weren't used to it. But they get all the old loose fat off of you.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Tell me about your boot camp experiences.

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Well, you did a lot of marching and you work one week out of three months doing extracurricular jobs like mess cooking, working in the galley, working in the boathouse, and in Lake Michigan and just different things.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Do you remember your instructors?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: No. It's been too long. I didn't know any of my -- excuse me -- chiefs or anything like that, the people that I went to school.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Was it hard to get through?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Was it hard to get through?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Was it hard what?

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Was it hard to make it through it?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Oh, no. Young kids got a lot of vim and vigor and vitality. Not like an old fellow.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: What wars did you serve in?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: What wars did you serve in?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: World War II and the Korean War.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Where did you go exactly?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Up around the Aleutian chain. I was on a tender. We took care of torpedoes and torpedo, you have to -- every year if you don't use it, within a year you have to tear it all down and apart and clean it all up, get the rust off of out it and everything. And when a ship pulls alongside, you'll overhaul torpedoes and took __+ and overhauled the ones that they didn't fire.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Do you remember the first time arriving on the ship?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Well, after I got out of school, I went up to Astoria, Oregon. There was a mouth at the Columbia River where the baby flattops would come by and I was supposed to be going to torpedo shop there, but the current messed everything up so they closed the place down. What they used to do is bring the -- they call them Kaiser Coffins, baby flattops and bring them down to the Columbia River from Portland where they build them and they would have the crews and everybody put on right there at the mouth of the Columbia River and send them on up to the Pacific Ocean. So then, uh, and they closed the shop and then there were nine of us that got sent up to Aleutian Islands, went aboard the U.S.A. Black Hawk. It was one of the oldest ships in the Navy. It was number six. At that time her top speed was, I think, six knots. Now it's ships and flattops and so on and so forth over 30 knots. So went into the torpedo shops and we'd wait for the ships to come in, whether they were destroyers or submarines and their ship would be ready to be overhauled and take cares and give them something that we had in storage to put back on the ship and that's what it was. It was just a tender that took care of everything. You had a big machine shop there. Somebody would want to get something down on the ship. As much time to send them back to the States or whatever, they could stop by and it was just an overhaul shop. Just like the car breaks down, you bring them over, and if it's close to the water district instead of turning everybody back over to the States, do the overhaul work, and did that about every day. Took the warheads off because they were all ready to go. They were loaded. Take them off and up in the hills in the magazine area and get through overhauling them and put them back on. It was routine and then the hours you worked any hours they wanted you to do. There's no such thing as 3:00 in the afternoon until 11:00 at night. You worked and you got up, between about 5:30, had breakfast, and you go to work. A lot of times you work until 10:00, 11:00, 12:00 o'clock. You didn't have any certain hours like you to do around here. I'm only going to work six hours. As long as the work was there and you knew how to do it.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: You were talking about the baby flattop. What's that?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Years ago it's a big flattop now. About -- what am I trying to say?

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Aircraft carrier?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Aircraft carrier. It takes years to build a ship. These baby flattops they were using the hulls of old merchant ships and they just put a top on it and used them for -- because they were lacking a lot of power early part of the war. And that's what they called it __+ A lot of them got torpedo. They called it Kaiser Coffin, Kaiser and company built them flattops and they called them Kaiser Coffin. They had to have something for emergency because like I say it takes too long to build them. Big aircraft carriers. These were just little, little things like in little post-it stamps in the water.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: How did you decide to become a torpedoman? Like were you given it or?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: They -- when you first go into the Navy, they give you tests, see what they want -- check to see if you got any mechanical aptitude or whatever, so they -- they assign where you go or what you're going to do, so I didn't decide. The Navy decided and I didn't decide. They decided whether if you were good as a clerk, they Navy made you a clerk. You work in the storage area, you're doing everything in the storage area. That's how it worked. So then they would send you to school. We went for four months and made third class torpedoman and then they send me to advanced school and it was another four months. So it was about eight months going to school and stuff during the war and __++. They sent me to work and then I became a torpedoman. I have no idea what it consisted of or anything like that and there I was.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Where were the schools that they sent you to?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: San Diego, California.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Both of them?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Um, were you excited when you first, um, after when you went first went down to work on the boats? Like, was it, were you excited about it or it was just?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: No, no, no. You took everything in stride, you know. You knew what you had to do and so on and so forth. There wasn't fanfare or play. You knew either you do the job right or they'll get somebody to do it. And it wasn't at times you had fun, but when you you're overseas, there's no place to go. When you got through working and had supper, or whatever you want to call it, and then you maybe play a little cards and then went to bed. Lights out easily 9:00, 9:30. You get your sleep and so on and so forth. And you're up at 5:00, 5:30 in the morning, had breakfast and exercised. You kept in shape, exercises.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: What would happen if you didn't do your work? Like, what if you're a slacker?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Well, a lot of times they'd give you a little -- I don't know. What did they do. Punishment. I mean if you're, like, going to school and stuff, you only had a couple of days off during that time on liberty. If you screwed around and messed up, they'd take your liberty away from you. Like staying on the station or whatever, you couldn't do anything.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Was liberty like a break?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Yeah, a break.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Like a weekend?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Like a weekend or in the evenings a lot of times, you had port and (?) starboard(?) Half of the guys were in port and half in (?) starboard(?). You did guard duty when you had the duties and wherever you stayed, you always had the fire watch. Guys would be on the fire watch make sure no fire started, emergency. But when aboard ship, when you're aboard ship, you're out there. No place to go. Go in your bunk and did your work. You had a lot of goof-offs. A lot of guys who didn't do their share or pull their duties, but not much you can do about it. I mean you got -- a lot of them tried to get out of the Navy and stuff like they do brig time and so on and so forth. If they were goofing up all the time, they'd get a BCD, bad conduct discharge. They would get rid of them.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Well, where would you go if you got one of those? Would you just be allowed to go home?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: You went home, yeah. You messed up your living in America. They took away some of your rights of voting --

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Oh, really?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: -- and so on and so forth. Yes, sure. Nobody was striving for that. Mostly people, you always somebody hooting and hollering and complaining, but there's not much you can do about it.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: What were some of the punishments on the ships, like if you messed up on the ships?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: If you messed up on the ship, you just, well, they give you a little more extra duty, guard duty or cleanup duty. Compartment where you slept and so on and so forth. Different things. They had strings of different things they could do, you know. So, yeah, you didn't have too many goof-ups, but once in a while you had some. Like I said if they wanted to get out of the Navy, they'd get out of the service. Keep screwing up, screwing up, and finally they get sick and tired of it and out you go and send you home. If you got too nasty and stuff, they'd send you to the Navy brigs, help your __+, or someone, I think. If you goof up and they send you to the brigs __++ or whatever. So there's always boys getting rough. You just had to -- and you're overseas, what have you get to worry about? You can't go anywhere.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: When people got sent off the ship, did they, like -- how did they get them? Did an airplane fly in to an aircraft carrier nearby and take them away or --

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Oh, no, no.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: -- did your whole ship have to go back? How did they --

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: No, no.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: -- get sent back?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: They would send you -- well, a lot of ships going back and forth. So a lot of them they were heading certain ways, whether to the States or what. Put in you shackles or whatever and put you on that ship and send you to __ Washington, one of the big stations. I think it's get you over there and they put you on the train and fly you over, wherever you were going. Where you ever you had to go. It was a discharge. A discharge and they'd send you on your way, give you a new suit good-bye. And then you couldn't go back to any branch of the service. You lose some of your voting rights.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Did you guys -- did you ever see any combat? Like where did you ever have any planes where --

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: It's like most of your tenders and everything you were always back because if something happens, they wouldn't want your ship to get sunk or messed up, so you'd stay back for hundreds of miles.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: What was your most memorable experience?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: My most what?

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Memorable -- memorable experience.

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Oh, I don't know. Many experiments, thrills, ups and downs. Just a little bit of everything.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Well, what's a couple that stick out in your mind?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Oh, it's been so long that I don't even remember. It's been, let's see about 60 years anyway.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: How did you stay in touch with your family?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Well, the only way to stay touch with your family was by mail. There were no phone calls or anything like that. You just write. Some guys wrote once a week. I wasn't too much in writing so. They knew where I was or close by. You could never, when you write letters and stuff, you never told where you were because they would check your mail and if you had anything, they would scratch it out and they didn't want anybody to where you were because they're too many nosey people. Slip of the lip sink the ship was one of the things. But they knew where I was. I was being taken care of. You didn't need any money. You couldn't spend it on anything. Maybe once in a while I would buy a candy bar or cigarettes. Cigarettes I was paying a nickel a pack. Cigarettes now are more than five dollars a pack.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: What was the food like?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Food was -- was pretty good. I mean it wasn't the fanciest at times, but it was nourishing. They had somebody knew what they were doing. And you ate maybe I'd say if you didn't like this, or you didn't like that, but it was best for you. You had just to figure all this out. But most of the food was pretty good. One of the first meals I ever had was baked beans for breakfast. I never had baked beans for breakfast. My first meal in the Navy was baked beans and they served that twice a week, twice a week. And but overall the food was always good, you know.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Do you think your food was better than the food that the people on the frontlines got?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. Because they guys on the frontline and stuff like that had sea rations and they had canned stuff like, you know, Spam and stuff like that because they could only have the fixed food. Were meals, but they were cooks and stuff. Some would cook it and some would cook it. So we didn't eat too many sandwiches or different things. The guys in the frontline, they would get Spam and things like that. Overall the food was good.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Did you come in contact with a lot of guys that were actually fighting? Did you talk to a lot of guys?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: No, not too many. Like I say we were in the background just worrying about. I talked to guys who pulled up alongside, whether it was at cruiser or a destroyer or submarine, like I said, take their fish off and put torpedoes on and we would discuss things. It was always hurry up, hurry up. There was no lollygagging. You didn't mess around or B.S. or anything like that. They pulled up alongside they were like hooting and hollering and get this thing and get this thing. There they go after they change their torpedoes, they'd take off. And they weren't half a dozen or so, just individuals that were beating the odds a little bit and when it was their turn to come in because we didn't wanted to get a bunch of people and somebody find out bomb here or whatever, so anyway. And there always submarines around. So you had to take care of whatever.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Did you know anybody that died during the war?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Did you know anybody that died during the war?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Did I know anybody that what?

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: That died during the war.

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Oh, some of my friends, yeah. I knew a lot of, a lot of kids were, pals and somebody was __+. But it happened and nothing you can do it about, you know.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Did you make any friends you stayed in contact with after the war?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: I still stay in contact with one kid that was from Buffalo, New York. Thomas W. He and I still visit one another and contact with one another. The rest of them, everybody goes their way and gets married or whatever, goes to school, and that's it.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Was he on your ship or on a different ship?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: No. He and I were both on the same ship. That's why we got closer together. He and I -- 60, 65 years.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Did you feel, did you ever have any, like, traders on your boat or any spies on your ship?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: You don't know this and you don't worry about things like that. There are people around, yeah. We had problems one time. They were drinking torpedoes, which was alcohol. In the Navy we had a little bit of beer, but we didn't have any booze or anything like that. We had called it the sneaky parties for a little celebrating and whatnot and this kid got really inebriated and they threw him in his bunk and he tried to vomit and he couldn't. He choked himself. He died. So then they said, you know, there's so much going here, this guy leaves, this guy comes, and so on and so forth. And then they send somebody to find out what happened. Like if a guy from the FBI or from whatever, and they soon find out, you know. They asked different guys question. A guy slips once in a while what happened. You find out what happened. You try to keep quiet and sometimes it doesn't help.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Did you feel a lot of pressure or stress during the war on you?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: No. I always just, hey, if it's going to happen, it's going to happen. You don't go around worry. A lot people, they going to die. So what? What are you going to do about it? Everybody has to die. That's one thing -- I mean you thought of it. You're still a young man at that time, only 22, 23 years old. You know, I got a long time to live hopefully, but something happens where you.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Was there anything that you did for like good luck or anything?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: I didn't believe in luck. I'm not one who just sits around and says, man, my luck remember, this is my good luck charm. The good Lord took care of me and did a good job. That's all I can say. I wasn't the type that was religious. But I know there's somebody higher than me that takes care of me. If you want to be taken care of, you know, so. Just like now, I never thought I'd reach 78 years old. Do you know what I mean. But it's happened. I don't know how much longer I can go. I mean right now I feel like not worth a plum nickel, but you don't know. You play it -- excuse me -- by ear and a day at a time, you know. You only you get up in the morning and you say, well, I'm still on this side of the grass. Well, like I said I don't worry about if I'm going to die. I've lived long enough. I'd like to just watch my grandkids grow up a little more. You, watch you wrestle. Have Nick his craft and the girls or whatever, Jake. You want to see them, but if it's not there, it's not there. You don't worry about it. I don't anyway. I don't know. I don't know. It's -- sometimes it's a cruel world, but you got to go with the flow. That's all I got to say.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Were there anybody -- did anybody ever like come on your ship to like entertain you guys? Like?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Not so much on the ship. Our ship wasn't -- you -- we were tied up a little ways and you got in the whale boat and come into shore, hit the base, and then we'd have entertainment there or movie stars and orchestra and band.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Do you remember any famous people that you saw or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Do you remember any famous people or any famous bands that you saw or anything?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Not anymore. Like I said, never bothered me and I didn't, you know. It was good. Broke the monotony of some of the things, but.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Did you guys tell each other stories on the boat? Like, did everybody pretty much know about everybody else or did you guys --

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Oh, yeah, yeah. You always -- no matter how many guys you know, new guy comes and where you from and so on and so forth. B.S. and B.S. and B.S., you know. We -- excuse me. Played a lot of cards, pinochle mostly. Once in a while you played some poker. 25, 50-cent pot limit and so on and so forth because we didn't make that kind of money. You have to give -- you've got to make first class torpedoman probably making $110 a month, so. And like I said aboard ship, we'd have __ locker always. That's where you buy ice scream and cigarettes and so on and so forth and so on. It didn't go too far. Not that much money. It's better than nothing, you know. They took care of your -- they took care of your food and your bedding and everything else and just took care of what you like if you wanted to smoke, smoke. You had to buy them. They didn't give them to you. Once in a while have a milkshake or once in a while they have a couple of beers. You have to go back to the shore. They had a beer hall there. Beer was probably ten cents a bottle or whatever. Cigarettes for five cents a pack.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: How, like, how long in between would have you a break when you would go to the shore? Like how long did you work in between when you had a break?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Oh, probably a couple of three weeks.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Three weeks?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Yeah. You didn't go too much time off. Too much hustle and bustle. It was the earlier part of the war, too. You had to take care of those in front of you, you know. It wasn't a pleasure trip or a cruise on one of the yachts or anything.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Did you ever get to go home during the war and then come back on like leave or anything?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: When I got out of torpedo school, I wanted to come home for a few days, but they only gave me seven, eight days. I couldn't get a flight out of San Diego to come home and I sure wasn't going to get on the train because it took about four or five days from San Diego to home. Didn't have enough time, so when I left in March I was gone for about three years. And then just about when the war was over, which I didn't know was going to happen, but we knew it was going to be pretty close. I put in for to go to electric school -- torpedo school. And, uh, and that's -- what am I trying to say? Across the bay, big submarine base there. I put in for __ torpedo school and they flew me to (?) Burlington (?), Washington and from there they gave me 30 days leave and as far as I knew I was going to go to school and then the war ended. So I'm at home and I get a letter to report to Cleveland and they'll tell you what's going on. And after my 30 days, I reported to Cleveland and they said if you sign up for another six years in the Navy, you can go to school. At that time I was 21, 22, or 23, I said no, I'll take my chances. They said okay. They sent me to Miami, Florida. And that was a big hub and I was the in seventh naval district. They made me shore patrolman which was nice. They used to get on the bus from Miami and go down to Key West, Florida stay over night, and then back up the next day and the sailors were going back and forth. So then they sent me to up Cocoa, Florida, which is Banana River Naval Air Station as a shore patrolman. So I stayed there for two or three months and they said, well, you can go home. They're going to discharge you and you're not going to go to school because I didn't want to sign for six years and so on and so forth. It was November or December they said, "Do you want to go home?" And I said, "Can I extend a little bit?" I said, "It's cold at home." I stayed another six months. So signed up for another six months and I stayed. I was shore patrol for that time.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: What did you do on your shore patrol?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Make sure nobody got in trouble. But if you get troublemakers who are off drinking and raising hell, so you took care of it, tried to break up fights, whatever.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Were there a lot of fights?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Oh, in the beer joints, you betcha. You got a drunken marine or soldier or sailor. Half of the time they didn't know what the hell they were doing. Yeah, we're fighting over women. We had to be the middleman and try to separate them. And if they don't listen, throw them in the paddy wagon and took them to the station and for a day or two. That was it.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Did you ever -- did you like patrol and make sure no one snuck in the country or?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Do what?

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Did you have to patrol and make sure no one snuck into the country or was that not your job?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: No. The guys around Cocoa, I took care of them. You didn't worry about things like. FBI or whoever took care of worrying about all major things, you know. We took care of minor things, a little scrapes, and so on and so forth.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: How many other shore patrolmen were there?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Down there, probably 20, 30 of us worked different shifts. During the daytime we only had one guy who worked from 8:00 to 4:00 because everybody was working at the station and then liberty called and everybody else was working with us because a lot of them would come into town and so on and so forth. And I used to ride the bus Orlando from Cocoa to um, um, Orlando. They had a bus come from the station to Orlando because Cocoa was nothing. It was just one horse town. That horse was dead. So as you go to Orlando on liberty, it's a much bigger town, more women, whatever, attractions. There were good times and bad times. More good times than bad times as far as I'm concerned.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Do you recall any like anything that funny that happened during your service any time, like, anything that was really, like, ironic or anything?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Nothing extremely funny, but I saw a lot of the sailors and marines and so on and so forth get killed on their boozing.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: On their boozing?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: I'd be in paddy wagon and you'd get a call at such and -- you had an accident at such and such place. And you'd get up there and three or four servicemen killed in their stupidity trying to go 80, 90 miles an hour. I was trying to direct traffic one time. I looked up and there this car was really highballing it, had one of those big long flashlights with the red parker and I'm waving at them to slow them down and everything. They just about got near me and I threw it at that them. Hit the passenger and they finally stopped. It's just over in __+ there was already an accident there, a couple fatalities. So, you know, you get boozing, the people they don't what's going on.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Did you ever pull a lot of pranks?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Did you ever pull a lot of pranks?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Oh, yeah. We had a little fun. Different things. Yeah, like one of the pranks a guy would be sleeping and have his hand hanging out and we'd get a warm bucket of water and stick his hand in and he'd wet himself. That was one of the old tricks. Different things.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Did you take a lot of pictures while you were there during the war?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Aboard ship, there was nothing to take. I took a few. You couldn't send them home because --

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Well, they didn't want us to know where we are. Somebody might intercept it. So they wouldn't let you, so no use taking pictures. I got a few probably that I had took. But once in a while, we'd go up to the river, go fishing, trout fishing, probably hoarding trout. And you go and get it. And we'd take maybe 15, 20 guys, go over to the galley and get bread and butter and had a little cooking oil in what we called it, had a little cook stove, and fry fish and drink a few beers and pass the time away that did.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: What did you think of like everybody that you worked with in the Navy? Like most people were good people or?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Most of the time everybody was good. There are few assholes. I shouldn't say assholes. These people, no matter what you did for them, they didn't want to be helpful or things like that. Or if you was a loner like that, you know. So okay. I forgot what I want to say. More than one pebble on the beach. They didn't want to associate. They didn't want to be sociable. You go about your business. Leave them alone. Someway everyday life here, just like you in school, you know. You find somebody that's so tough there, and you know, somebody kicked the stuff out of them. You'll find it, you know. You live day to day, Ed. Hopefully you're doing right. A lot of times maybe you weren't. It's there.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Did you -- were you like -- were you friends with most of the people there on the ship?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Did I what?

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Were you friends with most of the people on the ship?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Most people like you?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: When you live with somebody 24 hours a day, you've got to be. You can't be a jerk or whatever word you want to use. If you want to be friendly, fine. If you didn't want to, who cares. There's somebody else there. You're not the only one. If you want to be a loner, be a loner. Don't bother me and I won't bother you. Just like everyday life. You know, at school you find these yahoos they think they know everything and they're just as dumb as everybody else. You've got to prove yourself in this world.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Did you keep a diary or anything or notes or anything?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: No, no, no. I -- I was never a good at that.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Did a lot of people?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Oh, yeah a lot of people every day. We did this. Well, it was Tom O'Neill I'm talking about. He had a girlfriend. And he used to write a letter to her every day. And I said to myself, what in the world is he writing about? Okay, so I love you from Tuesday to Wednesday. Two and three pages. Well, I got up this morning, I went to the bathroom, took a shower, brushed my teeth, went down to the galley, and ate breakfast, and we went and start to overhaul the torpedo. Felix is over there doing this and I'm over here doing that. Same routine. Do you know what I mean? So I would think whoever was receiving that letter, same B.S., same old stuff there.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Did he get a lot of letters back from her?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Did he get a lot of letters?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: She wrote him every day. It was one of those there were of few of them in the service like that.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Did he end up marrying her?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Married and never had any children of his own, but he adopted a couple. He had several kids, a boy and a girl, I think. And he was a policeman, an Irish fellow. He was a policeman in Buffalo, New York. He was retired. And I wrote maybe four or five lines. I'm okay. Once a month and that was enough. I didn't have any girlfriend. I wasn't worried about who I was going to marry or anything else. I never even knew Marge. I didn't know Marge until I got out of the service or I was home on leave.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Do you remember the day you found out that you were going to have to go back to war or?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Do you remember the day you found out you were going to have to go back into the service? Like did you --

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: I got out of the service, Edward, in November. I came home and I joined the reserves, the naval reserve. It was an acronym for the blimp hangars or the dirigible hangars. That was the naval air station. And I would go there two times a month and when the Korean War started, next day after the war started, I got a letter to come on back. So I'm going back in the Navy for two more years. Didn't go anywhere. Went to Norfolk, Virginia. He made me a policeman on the naval air station. They didn't need me any more than anything, but you were handy just in case they needed you. (Interruption caused by changing of tape.)

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: You were serving as a policeman down in Norfolk, Virginia?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Yeah. I was down there for not quite two years and then the war was over and so they sent a lot of us home. They didn't need us.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Were you excited about going home again?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Oh, yeah, because I had Steven. He was -- well, when I left he was five months old and I brought him and Marge down to Norfolk for about a year, and then the war was over, came back home, and I started working at -- I was working.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Why did you join the naval reserve after World War II?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: It was a little extra money for me. You get paid for it. And I always enjoyed the Navy. __++ I didn't think the Korean War was going to start. Hey, you don't why -- a lot of times and you think you do dumb things, I do dumb things. So if I knew the Korean War was going to drag me back in, I would have hung up in Florida and stayed home. You don't know. You take your chances. In other words, everyday life is a gamble, so just roll with the punches. That's about all you can do.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: When you joined the naval reserve, did you join that for life, like?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: No, no, no.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Or how long did you join it for?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: You join it for as longs as you want to. There are some people in the reserve for 25, 30 years. If you didn't want to, you just resign. Do you know what you mean. But.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Did you resign after the Korean War?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Yeah. That was before I got discharged, the guy says, "Do you want to join the reserve?" I says, "I wouldn't be here if you ask me that silly question." I said, I did it once. I don't want to make the same mistake twice, you know."

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Like I said I'm not sorry what happened or what had happened. It was just, just one of those things. Like breaking up with that old girlfriend or something, and you go back to her, you know.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Do you, do you like veteran work now or anything?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: I belonged to the VFW for a long time and American Legion and you help out veterans and so on and so forth. Now I'm lucky to take care of myself. I'm too damn old for a lot of that stuff.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: What did you do after the war? Like what was your career after the war?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Started back working Firestone building tires. I got tired of the night shift, so I quit there and I went over to Ohio __++ and started working for them. I worked 38 years for them and then retired. See, I could have gotten a free college education. A lot of guys went to school right after the war, you know. Uncle Joe went four years to college. And Uncle Sam took care of the bill and didn't cost you a penny if you go to school. And for some people school is good and other people didn't worry about it. You know, now it's your time now. When I was a kid, you got into the eighth grade, I was pretty good. And then later on was you had to have a high school education. Now in order to get a job and stuff, you've got to be a college graduate. Things are different. So but, or just like now a lot of guys kids your age out of high school and stuff, they join the reserves or the ROTC and stuff like that, and a couple of years, they've got money and their education is there if they want it if that's what they're striving for. And in today's times every little bit helps. Like being in the ocean. Every little bit helps. Every day the world and everything else changes, you know, and.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Did you ever think about becoming a policeman or anything that had to do with --

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Oh, there were a lot of things that strikes your mind, you know. You want to do this or want to be that. It's just like today's time. You're waiting to make that dollar, you know. Hopefully you get married, you get a good wife. You might get a lemon. You might, you know, like a lot of kids around here, five or six dollars an hour. Nobody wants work to for peanuts. Sit on your butt at home if you don't want to work for peanuts. You've got to start somewhere. If you don't have the mentality or whatever, you can still be sitting at home and that peanut job is still going to be open, you know. But if you've got a little guts and whatever doing your thing, go to school. A lot of people, you know, why should I waste four years in college for. The differential of that four years, you could be working for peanuts flipping hamburgers, do you know what I mean, or get yourself a job to that pays something and so and so forth. But a lot of people _+ so on and so forth. That's the way it goes.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Did your experiences in the Navy, like, did that change, like, your idea of about war or did that change --

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Well, you know, nobody likes the war and so and so forth. But when somebody kicks you in the butt, you've got to do something. Like in my time, they said war is hell. That's right. War is hell. What does it solve? You're still going to have people that don't do this and they don't do that. Or they don't like, you, whether it's your nationality or your beliefs or anything like that -- if you're an Italian or if you're a dumb Pollack. Hey, it's not going to change. Nah, I don't know, Edward. It's -- times are different. It's a cruel world. I've had people come up to me, well, I didn't tell them what's happening. I didn't come into this word. Who did? Did any of us? I never had anybody ask me if I want to come in world and face reality or whatever. It's there. If you don't like it, get yourself and gun and help yourself.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Did you ever attend any reunions or anything special?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Not anymore, no. I used to.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: You used to?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: I used to. We used to have a get together, but not anymore. And 80 percent of the people are gone. When you get between 70 and 80, you know, people die off like flies as far as I'm concerned. But it's like we're going to a class reunion, Marge's class reunion. We've been out of school for 65 years and we're going to -- yeah, 65 years. A lot of people don't want to come to the reunion. Hey, nobody's forcing you. I like to go and then see people you haven't seen for 20 or 30 years. Say hi and how are you and so on and so forth. I like to B.S. with people. We were on the golf course one time and five, six, seven years ago or longer than that. Anyway we were sitting in the clubhouse, there were four of us who used to go golfing every Monday. And four guys walked in and I looked and I said, "I know that guy." And he said, "Well, how do you know him?" I said, "He and I were in boot camp." And that was about 30, 45 years, lapse time. I said, "He was in my boot camp." And he was originally from Cleveland or what was I trying to say. I don't know where. Suburbs of Cleveland. I want to say Norwalk, but it wasn't Norwalk. But anyway, and the guys sitting there and he says, "Well, how are you going to know? I said, "I'm going to go over there and ask him and he'll either say yes or no." People were afraid to ask. You've got a question and see something. I went over to him and I said, "I know your first name, but I can't remember your last name. Your name is Ted." He says, "Yeah." I said, "Were you in Company 432, boot camp?" He says, "I'll be a son of bitch." He said, "Do you remember me?" I said, "Yeah." And I find out his last name was Westerhold. I came back to the table and anyhow. How are you going to find out? You go ask him. Oh, yeah. There are times. It's like well, Friday we had at the men's club and dinner and stuff, a couple of guys kept looking at me and said, "What's the matter?" Do you forget who I am? Some I haven't seen for like 10 or 15 years, but of course the beard throws a lot of them off. And sometimes you don't even remember from one day to the next. It's there.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Did -- did you ever -- the war, like how you participated in the war, does like affect anything about you now?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Do what now?

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Like do your experiences affect how you are now?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Do you think you'd still be the same person without it?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: No. You change from day it day, Ed. But it's not that big of a change. No, Ed. It doesn't change much. Once a dummy, always a dummy, you know, (laughter), or whatever you want to say.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Do you -- do you agree with like the war now that we're kind of getting into with Afghanistan, and do agree with like the war and everything we're getting into now or it's?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Any war, Edward, I'll be telling you. People lie and tell stories. You don't know what to believe. Do you know what I mean? This could have -- could have been averted or that could have been averted or, you know, leave the gate open and you lose everything. So I don't even want to worry about it. I worry about you and the rest of our grandkids and so on and so forth. It's the same way if I die tomorrow. I had a good life, good kids, and everything. That's why I tell you be yourself. Don't put on airs. Don't think you're a millionaire and you don't have a pot to piss in or a window to throw it out. Be yourself. I mean times, it's tough to be yourself. Somebody is telling you, well, you should have done this and you should have done that. Don't cry over spilt milk or water over the dam.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Is there anything you want to talk about that we haven't talked about?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Is there anything you want to talk about that we haven't talked about?

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Not especially, Edward. Excuse me. Any war is, you know, I don't feel up to snuff and can't do anything. Be soon I won't be able to tie my shoes or whatever. I'll be around.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: Thanks a lot, Granddad, for --

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: You're more than welcome.

sp.speaker: Ed LoBuglio
sp.p: -- helping me out.

sp.speaker: Felix Magier
sp.p: Just be a good boy.
